title: Theorem
body_md:
$$\mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\mathrm{CM}):{\mathbb Q})\cong\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}(\mathrm{CM})\le_\approx \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM}),$$
where $\le_\approx$ ("almost equal")
 means that for any finite set  $\bar{\tau}$ of square-free imaginary quadratics, for $\mathrm{CM}_{\bar{\tau}}=\bigcup \{ \mathrm{CM}_\tau: \tau\in \bar{\tau}\},$
$$ \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}(\mathrm{CM}_{\bar{\tau}})\le_\mathrm{open} \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM}_{\bar{\tau}}),$$ 
(open, and hence finite index subgroup).
head: manual
name: see \ref{MainGal}(i

title: Proof
body_md:
We use \cite{Milne0} again.
Note first that canonical models for $\mathrm{Sh}_{K(N)}(\mathrm{GL}_2, \mathbb{H})$ over the field $E(\mathrm{GL}_2, \mathbb{H})={\mathbb Q}$ exist according to Deligne \cite{Deligne}, see also \cite{Milne1}. In particular,  $\mathrm{S}_{K(N)}$ are defined over ${\mathbb Q}.$ (iii) follows sinse $\mathrm{S}$ is the limit of the $\mathrm{S}_{K(N)}$ and $E_K$ just defines the splitting into irreducible components of a curve over ${\mathbb Q}.$
  

                                           
  For $g\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\hat{{\mathbb Z}})$ we have 
$g\cdot K(N)\cdot g^{-1}=K(N)$ and hence by \cite{Milne0}, Theorem 13.6,
the maps 
$$s/K(N)\mapsto g*s/K(N)$$
are defined over ${\mathbb Q}.$  Since the action of $g$ on $S$ is the limit of its actions on the $S_{K(N)}$
 (i) follows.


(ii)  follows from  \cite{Milne0}, Theorem 13.6 when one considers $g=1.$

   $\Box$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition $\tau= a\sqrt{-n}+b$ for some  $a,b\in {\mathbb Q}$ and a  positive square-free integer $n.$ Then
 $\tau= r \sqrt{-n}$ for $r=\left( \begin{array}{ll}
 a\ b\\
 0\ 1
\end{array}\right),$ that is $\tau \in  \mathrm{S}_{\sqrt{-n}}.$  

In order to prove uniqueness consider the assumption that
$[\sqrt{-m},g_1]=[\sqrt{-n},g_2]$ for a square-free positive integer $m$ and $g_1,g_2\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f).$ This is equivalent to 
$[\sqrt{-m},1]=[\sqrt{-n},g],$ for $g=g_2g_1^{-1}.$  By (\ref{qak}) the latter is equivalent to 
$$(\sqrt{-m},1)=(q\sqrt{-n},qg),\mbox{ for some }q\in \mathrm{GL}_2({\mathbb Q}),$$
that is $\sqrt{-m}=q\sqrt{-n}.$ This is possible only if $m=n.$ 

The uniqueness of representation follows. $\Box$
head: manual

label: rts
title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose 
$$[\tau, 1]^\sigma=[\tau, r_\tau(\sigma)], \mbox{ for some } r_\tau(\sigma)\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f),$$
and hence, for any $a\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f),$
 \begin{equation}\label{rts} [\tau, a]^\sigma=[\tau, 1\cdot a]^\sigma=a^{-1}\cdot [\tau,1]^\sigma= [\tau, r_\tau(\sigma)\cdot a].\end{equation}
 
\medskip


We claim that  $r_\tau(\sigma)\in N_\tau .$
                                      
Indeed, let $\tau$ be the fixed point of $q\in  \mathrm{GL}_2^+({\mathbb Q}),$ $q\notin Z({\mathbb Q}).$ Then by \ref{specpoints} $[\tau,1]$ is a fixed point of $q$ and $q^{-1}$ and so 
$$[\tau,q]=[\tau,1]\mbox{ and } [\tau, r_\tau(\sigma)\cdot q]=  
[\tau,r_\tau(\sigma)].$$ 

Hence $[\tau,r_\tau(\sigma)]$ is a fixed point of $q$ and thus by \ref{specpoints}(ii) $r_\tau(\sigma)\in N_\tau .$



Conversely, if $r\in N_\tau$ then for each $q\in G_\tau\setminus Z({\mathbb Q})$ there is $q'\in G_\tau,$ 
$$[\tau, r]=[\tau, q'r]=[\tau,rq]=q* [\tau,r].$$ 
                                                                                                                              
 
Define  the map $\sigma_{r,\tau}: \mathrm{S}_\tau\to \mathrm{S}_\tau,$  a partial transformation of $\mathrm{S},$   by setting
for each $a\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ 
$$[\tau,a]^{\sigma_{r,\tau}}:= [\tau,ra].$$
Then $\sigma_{r,\tau}$ trivially satisfies (\ref{autg}). Also  (\ref{aut0}) is satisfied   because $rq=q'r$. This proves that $\sigma_{r,\tau}$ acts as an automorphism on $\mathrm{S}_\tau$ and $r=r_\tau(\sigma_{r,\tau}).$
 

                                
                                      
                                                                       
Now note that by (\ref{qak})
$[\tau, r]=[\tau,1],$ for $r\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f),$ holds  if and only if 
$r\in G_\tau.$ This proves (\ref{rsig2}). 
 $\Box$
head: manual

label: GT1
title: Proof
body_md:
Compare the conclusion of \ref{rtsProp} with \cite{Milne0}, 12.8 describing the action on the special points $\mathrm{S}_\tau$  of the canonical model by
$\sigma\in \mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}(\tau)).$ 

In the notation of \cite{Milne0}, (60)-(62):

$\tau=x,$ ${\mathbb Q}(\tau)=E(x)$ and 
$T(\mathbb{A}_f)=T_\tau $ as in our \ref{S+}. Further
\begin{equation} \label{GT1} r_x: \mathbb{A}^\times_{{\mathbb Q}(\tau)}\ \ \to \  T(\mathbb{A}_f); \ \ a+b\tau\ \ \mapsto \ \ \left( \begin{array}{ll}
\ a\ nb\\ -b\ \ a
\end{array}\right).\end{equation}
                                                     
 
 Consequently, $r_\tau(\sigma)$ is the same as $r_x(s)$   of \cite{Milne0}, 12.8, for $s\in \mathbb{A}^\times_{{\mathbb Q}(\tau)}$ such that $\sigma=\mathrm{art}(s),$ the Artin symbol. 
 Thus the matrices $r_x(s)\in T_\tau $  of (\ref{GT1}) deliver all the Galois automorphism of $\mathrm{S}_\tau(\mathrm{CM})$ which fix
 ${\mathbb Q}(\tau).$ 
 
 Now let $\mathsf{i}: {\mathbb C} \to {\mathbb C}$ be  complex conjugation.
 $\mathsf{i}$ induces a non-trivial automorphism of ${\mathbb Q}(\tau)$ and an automorphism of $\mathrm{S}_\tau(\mathrm{CM}).$ 
 
Claim.  $\mathsf{i}$
                        
  corresponds to the action by an element
$$r_{\tau}(\mathsf{i})= \left( \begin{array}{ll}
-c\ nd\\ -d\ \ c
\end{array}\right)\in N_{\tau}\setminus T_{\tau}.$$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
The transformation $\eta: \mathbb{H}\cup \mathbb{H}^-\to \mathbb{H}\cup \mathbb{H}^-$
 induced on $\mathbb{H}\cup \mathbb{H}^-\subset \mathrm{S}$ by $\mathbf{i}$ is studied (in much more general setting) in
 \cite{MilneCC}. Lemma 3.2  of that paper states in particular
 that (in our notation $n:=\mathbf{d}_{-1}$), for $g\in \mathrm{GL}_2({\mathbb Q}),$    
 $$\eta([\tau,g])=[\tau,\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g].$$  
In particular, $$\eta(\tau)=\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot\tau.$$

It implies, as proved further in \cite{MilneCC}, Conjecture B (a form of Langlands' conjecture on complex conjugation): 
$$[\tau,g]^\mathbf{i}=[\eta(\tau),g]=[\tau,\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g]$$  
for all $g\in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f).$
 
 \medskip
 
Now let
  $\rho\in \mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}).$
                               
  Then, either it fixes  ${\mathbb Q}(\tau)$ and has the form (\ref{GT1}) or $\mathsf{i}\circ\rho$  fixes  ${\mathbb Q}(\tau)$ and so $\rho$ can be represented by the product of a matrix from 
  $T_{\tau}$ with the above  matrix from   $N_{\tau},$ which gives us again a matrix of the form $\left( \begin{array}{ll}
-c\ nd\\ -d\ \ c
\end{array}\right)$ from  $N_{\tau}.$ 
This concludes the proof of (i) and (ii).
head: manual
name: Claim

title: Proof
body_md:
Since
$$ (g*[\tau,a])^\sigma=([\tau,ag^{-1}])^\sigma=[\tau, rag^{-1}]=g*[\tau,a]^\sigma,$$
the set of special points in $C_g$ (the graph of $g$ on $\mathrm{S}$) is invariant under $\sigma.$ 
Hence the set of special points in the algebraic curve $C_{g,N}\subset \mathbb{Y}(N)\times \mathbb{Y}(N)$  is invariant under $\sigma.$ But the set of special points is Zariski dense in the special curve $C_{g,N},$ and hence $C_{g,N}$ is invariant under $\sigma.$ Finally, this implies $C_g,$ the limit of the $C_{g,N},$ is invariant under $\sigma.$

name: iii

title: Proof
body_md:
We have established in (iii) that $\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}$ satisfies (\ref{autg}), that is $s\mapsto g*s$ is definable in the structure. We conclude  by \ref{Fact2.6}
that
$\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}$ is an expansion of $\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}$ by possibly extra relations, which implies the embedding of the automorphism groups.
$\Box$
head: manual
name: iv

label: propE
title: Remark
body_md:
An important property of $\sigma$ is the {\bf preservation of connected components}, see \ref{Fact2.6}.
 Hence, for some $\mu=\mu(\sigma)\in \hat{{\mathbb Z}}^\times$
\begin{equation} \label{propE}\bigwedge_{i=1}^n\, [\tau_i, r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)]\in \mathrm{S}^\mu
\end{equation} 
\end{pkt}
\begin{pkt}\rm 
Let
$$\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}_{\bar{\tau}}$$
be the automorphism group of the pure structure on $\mathrm{S}_{\bar{\tau}}=\bigcup_{i=1}^n \mathrm{S}_{\tau_i}.$ By the remark \ref{2.5+} following the definition of $\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure},$ $\sigma$ acts on $\mathrm{S}_{\bar{\tau}}$ preserving the action of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ and the equivalence $E.$ The first is the condition (\ref{autg}) and the second (\ref{propE}). Since we represent the points of $\mathrm{S}$ as double-cosets we also need (\ref{aut0}).
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
(i) By the preservation of connected components property (\ref{propE}), given $\sigma$ there is a $\mu$ such that 
for each $\tau_i:= \sqrt{-m_i},$
$$[\tau_i, r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)]\in \mathrm{S}^\mu, \mbox{ and hence } \det r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)=q_i^{-1}\cdot\mu, \ \mu\in \hat{{\mathbb Z}}^\times, \mbox{ some } q_i\in {\mathbb Q}_+.$$

This proves the first statement of (i). For the second statement
                                                                                          
               
 use the fact that $\mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q})$ acts faithfully and transitively on the set of components $\mathrm{S}^\mu$ of $\mathrm{S}$ (see \cite{Milne1}, 3.4) so for each $\mu$ there is a $\sigma$ and $\bar{r}_{\bar{\tau}}(\sigma)$ such that  $\bigwedge_i \det r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)= q_i \mu.$ 
 
 
(ii) In matrix terms 
we have $$r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)=r_i=\left( \begin{array}{ll}\ a_i\ \ \ b_im_i\\ 
-\epsilon_i b_i\ \ \epsilon a_i
\end{array}\right),\ \ \ \det r_i=\epsilon_i  (a_i^2 + b_i^2m_i)=  q_i^{-1}\mu,\ ( a_i,b_i\in \mathbb{A}_f)$$
where $\epsilon_i$ is $+1$ if  $r_i\in T_{\sqrt{-m_i}}$  and $-1,$ if 
$r_i\in N_{\sqrt{-m_i}}\setminus T_{\sqrt{-m_i}}.$



As a result we have the equalities
\begin{equation}\label{q1} \epsilon_i q_i (a_i^2+b_i^2m_i)= \mu = \epsilon_j q_j (a_j^2+b_j^2m_j);
                                                                                      
\ i,j=1,\ldots,n.\end{equation}


Assume that $\epsilon_i=\epsilon_j.$ 
Then the equality between the algebraic expressions takes place for 
some $a_i,b_i,a_j,b_j\in {\mathbb R},$ not both $a_i,b_i$ zero, as well. By the Hasse principle, there are $s_i,t_i\in {\mathbb Q},\ \ i=1,\ldots, n$
such that not both $s_i,t_i$ zero and
\begin{equation} \label{q2}\epsilon_i q_i (s_i^2+t_i^2m_i)=\epsilon_j q_j (s_j^2+t_j^2m_j).\end{equation}


Consider, for $i=1,\ldots,n,$ the  matrices with rational entries,
 $$g_i=\left( \begin{array}{ll}\ s_i\ t_im_i\\ 
 -t_i\ \  s_i
\end{array}\right),$$
which by definition belongs to $G_{\sqrt{-m_i}}.$

By dividing the algebraic expressions of (\ref{q1}) on respective expressions of (\ref{q2}) we get
$$(a_i^2+b_i^2m_i)(s_i^2+t_i^2m_i)^{-1}=(a_j^2+b_j^2m_j)(s_j^2+t_j^2m_j),$$
and recalling the formula for $\det r_i$  
we have  $$\det r_i g_i^{-1}=\epsilon_i(a_i^2+b_i^2m_i)(s_i^2+t_i^2m_i)^{-1}=\epsilon_j(a_j^2+b_j^2m_j)(s_j^2+t_j^2m_j)^{-1}=
\det r_jg_j^{-1}.$$
Choose  representatives for $\bar{r}_{\bar{\tau}}(\sigma)$ modulo $G_{\bar{\tau}}$ as 
$$r_i:= r_i g_i^{-1}$$

Suppose $\epsilon_{i_1}=\ldots=\epsilon_{i_k}=1$ and $\epsilon_{i_{k+1}}=\ldots=\epsilon_{i_n}=-1.$

We get, for some $q\in {\mathbb Q}_+,$ from above that
$$\begin{array}{lll}\det r_{i_1}=\ldots=\det r_{i_k} \mbox{ and }r_{i_1}\in T_{i_1},\ldots,r_{i_k}\in T_{i_k}\\
\det r_{i_{k+1}}=\ldots=\det r_{i_n} \mbox{ and }r_{i_{k+1}}\notin T_{i_{k+1}},\ldots,r_{i_n}\notin T_{i_n}\\
\det r_{i_1}=\ldots=\det r_{i_k}=q\det r_{i_{k+1}}=\ldots=q\det r_{i_n}
\end{array}
$$ 

(iii) The condition $\bar{r}=\langle r_1,\ldots,r_n\rangle\in \prod_i N_{\tau_i} $
implies that $\bar{r}$ determines a transformation of $\mathrm{S}_{\bar{\tau}}$ which satisfies (\ref{autg}) and (\ref{aut0}). The conditions (\ref{riri2}) implies that $\bar{r}$ satisfies (\ref{propE}). Thus the transformation belongs to $\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}_{\bar{\tau}}.$
$\Box$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
By \ref{AutC/F}(ii)
 ${\mathbb Q}(\mathrm{CM}_{\tau_i})={\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}.$ Hence
 ${\mathbb Q}(\bigcup_{i=1}^n\mathrm{CM}_{\tau_i})=\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}.$


Elements $\sigma$ of $\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}_{\bar{\tau}}$ by construction act on  $\bigcup_i\mathrm{CM}_{\tau_i}$   as an automorphism group of the field, hence 
$$\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}_{\bar{\tau}}\cong \mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}: {\mathbb Q}).$$ 

By \ref{Cor316} and definitions  $\bar{N}^{\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}} $ is isomorphic to the subgroup of the group of transformations 
 $\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}_{\bar{\tau}}$ induced by Galois automorphisms of ${\mathbb Q}(\mathrm{CM}_{\bar{\tau}})$ over ${\mathbb Q},$ which is exactly $\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}_{\bar{\tau}}.$ This proves the second isomorphism.
$\Box$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
First we claim that as groups of transformations, for each $i,$
$$\mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab})\cong \bar{T}^{0,\mathrm{Gal}}_{\tau_i} $$ via
 the canonical map
$$\sigma\mapsto \bar{r}_{\bar{\tau}}(\sigma).$$
In order to prove it note that  
$T^0_{\tau_i}\cong \mathbb{A}^0_{ {\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)}$ where  $\mathbb{A}^0_{ {\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)}$
is the  group of finite  ${\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)$-adeles of ${\mathbb Q}$-norm 1.
Now    
the isomorphism $$\mathbb{A}^0_{ {\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)}/\pm 1\cong \mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab}),$$
a corollary to Artin's reciprocity law, completes the proof of our claim. 



Now the definition of $\bar{T}^{0,\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}} $ 
together with the second statement of \ref{318-} and the claim above gives us
$$\bar{T}^{0,\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}}\cong  \left( \mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau_1)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab})\times \ldots \times \mathrm{Gal}({\mathbb Q}(\tau_n)^\mathrm{ab}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab})\right)\cap \mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:{\mathbb Q}).$$
It is easy to check using the definition of  $\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}$
that the right-hand side of the latter is exactly $\mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab}).$

Thus
$$\bar{T}^{0,\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}}\cong \mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:{\mathbb Q}^\mathrm{ab}).$$




For the proof of the second statement of the Lemma we use the proof of the adelic Mumford-Tate conjecture for the product of CM elliptic curves, \cite{Cadoret--Moonen} and \cite{Ullmo--Yafaev}.

Let ${\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}}$ denote the $\mathbb{Q}$-torus such that ${\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}}(\mathbb{A}_f)=T^*_{\bar{\tau}}$. We can form a CM-Shimura datum $({\bf T}*_{\bar{\tau}},\{h\})$ associated with a product $E_1\times\cdots\times E_n$ of elliptic curves, with $E_i$ having CM by $\mathbb{Q}(\tau_i)$. As in \cite{Ullmo--Yafaev},  Remark 2.8, for any neat compact open subgroup $K$ of $T^*_{\bar{\tau}}$ and $L$ a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}(\bar{\tau})$ such that $[h,1]\in{\rm Sh}_{K}({\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}},\{h\})(L)$, we obtain a homomorphism
\[\rho:{\rm Gal}(\bar{L}/L)\to K,\]
which describes the action of ${\rm Gal}(\bar{L}/L)$ on the fiber of
\[{\rm Sh}({\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}},\{h\})\to{\rm Sh}_{K}({\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}},\{h\})\]
over $[h,1]$ (which is a $K$-torsor). In particular, $\rho$ factors through the quotient ${\rm Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:L)$.

As explained on the following page of \cite{Ullmo--Yafaev}, $\rho$ yields the ${\rm Gal}(\bar{L}:L)$ representation on the Tate-module of $E_1\times\cdots\times E_n$. Take $L$ to satisfy $ {\mathbb Q}(\bar{\tau})\subseteq L\subset\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}.$
By \cite{Cadoret--Moonen}, Theorem A (ii), provided $h_\mathbb{R}$ is ``maximal'' (see Definition 2.1), the latter has open image in $T^*_{\bar{\tau}}$ and, therefore,
\[{\rm Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:L)\cap T^0_{\bar{\tau}}={\rm Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:L\mathbb{Q}^{\rm ab})\]
(the equality due to the fact that $T^0_{\bar{\tau}}$ is the kernel of the determinant map $T^*_{\bar{\tau}}\to\mathbb{A}^\times_f$) is open in $T^0_{\bar{\tau}}$.

To see that $h_\mathbb{R}$ is maximal, let $\sigma_i$ and $\bar{\sigma}_i$ denote distinct embeddings of $\mathbb{Q}(\tau_i)$. The cocharacter group of ${\bf T}^*_{\bar{\tau}}$ is equal to the set of elements 
\[\sum_{i=1}^n a_i\sigma_i+b_i\bar{\sigma}_i\]
such that $a_i+b_i$ is independent of $i$. It has a basis consisting of the $\sigma_i-\bar{\sigma}_i$, for $i=1,\ldots,n$, and $\mu$, where $\mu=\sum_i\sigma_i$ is the cocharacter associated with $h$. The ${\rm Gal}(\bar{\mathbb{Q}}:\mathbb{Q})$-orbit of $\mu$ consists of the sums of $n$ elements in which, for each $i$, the sum includes either $\sigma_i$ or $\bar{\sigma}_i$. Since 
\[\sigma_i-\bar{\sigma}_i=\mu-(\Sigma_{j\neq i}\sigma_j+\bar{\sigma}_i),\] the result follows from the the paragraph following Definition 2.3 of
\cite{Cadoret--Moonen}. $\Box$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
$\det/{\mathbb Q}_+(r_1,\ldots,r_n)$ takes its values in $\mathbb{A}_f^\times/{\mathbb Q}_+^\times\cong \hat{{\mathbb Z}}^\times.$  
It
 is well-defined by the definitions of 
$\bar{N}^{\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}} $ and $\bar{N}^*_{\bar{\tau}} ,$
and is surjective on both lines by \ref{TT1}(i). 
The kernel of $\det/{\mathbb Q}_+$ consists of tuples $\bar{r}$ of matrices $r_i=\left( \begin{array}{ll}
a_i\ \ b_im_i\\
-b_i\ a_i
\end{array}\right)$ such that $\det r_i=a_i^2+m_ib_i^2=q_i\in {\mathbb Q}^+,$ where $a_i,b_i\in \mathbb{A}_f.$ By the Hasse principle there exists $s_i,t_i\in {\mathbb Q}$ such that $s_i^2+m_it_i^2=q_i$ and thus there exists $g_i\in G_{\tau_i}$ such that $\det r_ig_i^{-1}=1.$ Thus $\bar{r}\in   \bar{T}^0_{\bar{\tau}}.$

It follows that the kernel
is $\bar{T}^{0,\mathrm{Gal}}_{\bar{\tau}}$ in the top line and
$\bar{T}^0_{\bar{\tau}}$ in the bottom line. $\Box$

head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
By  \ref{318} and \ref{Cor321} $\bar{N}^\mathrm{Gal}_{\bar{\tau}} $ 
acts on the compositum $\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}$ of the fields ${\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}$ as its
Galois group over ${\mathbb Q}.$  At the same time coordinate-wise  $\bar{r}=\langle r_1,\ldots,r_n\rangle\in N^*_{\bar{\tau}}$ acts on
the $i$-th coordinate by $[\tau_i,a]\mapsto [\tau_i, r_i a],$ which by  \ref{12.8} corresponds to the Galois action on ${\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}.$ Moreover, $r_i(\sigma) \in T_{\tau_i} $ if and only if $\sigma$ fixes $\tau_i$ in ${\mathbb Q}(\tau_i)^\mathrm{ab}.$  If $r_i(\sigma) \notin T_{\tau_i} $ then $r_i(\sigma)$ acts on $T_{\tau_i} $ by conjugation as $\mathbf{d}_{-1}.$

Let $\delta\in \{ 1,-1\}^n$ be an arbitrary sequence with values $\pm 1.$
The condition of independence of  the $\tau_i$ guaranties the existence of $\sigma_\delta\in \mathrm{Gal}(\mathrm{F}_{\bar{\tau}}:{\mathbb Q})$ such that 
$$\sigma_\delta(\tau_i)=\tau_i \Leftrightarrow \delta(i)=1.$$
Thus
$$ r_i(\sigma_\delta)\in T_{\tau_i} \Leftrightarrow \delta(i)=1.$$
It implies that 
 $$\bar{r}(\sigma_\delta)/T^\mathrm{Gal}_{\bar{\tau}} =\bar{r}(\sigma_{\delta'})/T^\mathrm{Gal}_{\bar{\tau}} \Leftrightarrow \delta=\delta'.$$
 $\Box$

head: manual

label: gD0
title: Proof
body_md:
By definition
\begin{equation}\label{gD0} [\tau,g\Delta]^\sigma=[\tau,r_\tau(\sigma)\cdot g\Delta].\end{equation}

We need to show that for $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}$ the condition
\begin{equation}\label{gD} [\tau,g\Delta]^\sigma=[\tau,g\Delta]\end{equation}
for all $\tau\in \mathbb{H}$ quadratic and all $g\in \mathrm{GL}_2 ,$ implies that
$\sigma$ is  the identity (recall the notation in \ref{Del}). 


We assume first that in (\ref{gD}) $\sigma$ acts trivially on $\mathrm{S}_\approx.$ $g=1$ and
 that $\tau=\sqrt{-n}.$  
 
 By definition
$$[\tau,1]^\sigma=[\tau,r], \mbox{ for some }r=
\left(\begin{array}{ll}
\pm a\ \pm nb\\ -b\ \ \ \ a
\end{array}\right)$$
It follows $r\in \Delta$ and hence $b=0$ and $a=1,$ that is $r=\mathbf{d}_{-1}$ or the identity. We assume, towards a contradiction, that $\sigma$ acts non-trivially on $S_{\tau}$ and thus $r=\mathbf{d}_{-1}$.

Now for the more general case we have with the same $r$
$$[\tau,g]^\sigma=[\tau,r\cdot g]=[\tau,q\cdot r\cdot g]$$
for any $q\in G_{\tau}$
and thus (\ref{gD}) implies 
$$g^{-1}\cdot q\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g\in \Delta,\mbox{ for some }q\in G_{\tau} $$
But $\det q\in {\mathbb Q}_+$ and  $\det g^{-1}\cdot q\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g=\det q\mathbf{d}_{-1}$ is a negative rational number. In $\Delta$ this is only satisfied for  $g^{-1}\cdot q\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g=\mathbf{d}_{-1}.$ 


Thus $q\mathbf{d}_{-1}=\left(\begin{array}{ll}
-a\ - nb\\ -b\ \ \ \ a
\end{array}\right)\in  \mathrm{GL}_2({\mathbb Q}).$ This is an involution only when $b=0$ and $a=\pm 1.$ Now the extra condition 
$g^{-1}\cdot q\mathbf{d}_{-1}\cdot g=\mathbf{d}_{-1}$ for all $g$ gives the final contradiction. $\Box$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
First note that any coset $a\Delta\subset \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f),$ $a\in  \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f),$
contains exactly one element of determinant in ${\mathbb Q}_+.$ The uniquiness of the representation  (\ref{srep}) follows.

The action (\ref{sact}) is well-defined because of the uniquiness of $a$ and the fact that $\det g\in {\mathbb Q}_+.$

Finally, note that the action (\ref{sact}) is isomorphic to the action of $g$ on the component $\mathrm{S}^1$ of $\mathrm{S},$ which according to \ref{specpointsapprox}(b) represents the action of $g$ on $\mathrm{S}_\approx.$
$\Box$

title: Warning
body_md:
Although both  $\tilde{\mathrm{G}}=\Delta({\mathbb Q}_+)\cdot \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$
and $\Delta'(\mathbb{A}_f)$ act on $\mathrm{S}_\approx,$ the action does not extend to the group $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ generated by the two subgroups.
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
(b) proves one direction. In the opposite direction use the fact that by definition 
$$t_i=[\tau_i, r_i\cdot a_i\cdot \det r_i^{-1}]_\approx=[\tau_i, r_i\cdot a_i]_\approx$$
where $\det r_1=\det r_2 \in \Delta.$ By \ref{Cor316} there is $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}$ such that
$r_i=r_{\tau_i}(\sigma)$ modulo ${\mathbb Q}_+.$ Using the Hasse principle as in the proof of \ref{TT1}(ii) we can make this an equality. This proves the claim.

                                                                       

\end{pkt}





       

\begin{pkt}\rm  \label{Hpure}
 It is  useful to think of the structure $\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}_\approx$ as the structure on the universe $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ which by  (\ref{Sapprox}) can be identified with $\mathrm{S}_\approx.$ The group $\tilde{\mathrm{G}}$ acts on $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ but the action is defined up to  inner automorphisms  as described in \ref{specpointsapprox}A(c). The other relations on $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ described in \ref{specpointsapprox}, B - E, determine a structure on $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ which we call $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}.$ 
 

\medskip
head: manual

title: Definition
body_md:
$\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ is the structure with two universes (sorts) $\mathrm{S}_\approx$ 
and $\tilde{\mathrm{G}}$ (the set $\mathrm{S}_\approx$ will also be called  $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$);
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
By definition, see (\ref{defSapprox}), we need to prove                                                                            
that  any automorphism of $\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}$ induces an automorphism of $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ and, conversely, any automorphism of  $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$
 can be lifted to an automorphism of 
$\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}.$ The former is proved in \ref{specpointsapprox}. So we need to show that any  
$\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\,\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ can be lifted to an automorphism $\rho$ of 
$\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}.$ 

Claim. {\em Any 
$\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\,\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM})$ can be lifted to an automorphism $\rho$ of 
$\mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM}).$ }
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider special points
$s_1,\ldots,s_n,\ldots\in \mathrm{S}_\approx$ with representatives \linebreak
$[\tau_1, a_1],\ldots,[\tau_1, a_n],\ldots\in \mathrm{S},$
$$\sigma: s_i\mapsto t_i,\ \ t_i=[\tau_i,b_i]_\approx, \mbox{ canonical representatives}.$$ 

 
                                                                      
                     
Since $\sigma$ preserves $R,$ we get 
$$\vDash  R(s_1,s_i,t_1,t_i), \mbox{ for }i=1,...,n,...$$
and hence
$$b_i=r_i\cdot a_i\cdot \det r_i^{-1},\ r_i\in N_{\tau_i}, \ \det r_1=\det r_i, \mbox{ for }i=1,...,n...$$
By  \ref{Cor316} there is a $\rho\in  \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM})$ such that $r_i=r_{\tau_i}(\rho),$ $i=1,...,n...$,  and hence
$$s_i^\sigma=t_i=[\tau_i,b_i \Delta]=[\tau_i,a_i\Delta]^\rho=s_i^\rho,\ \ i=1,...,n... $$
Claim proved.
                                                                                                  
 
Note that the last argument in the proof of the claim also shows that $\bigwedge_i R(s_1,s_i,t_1,t_i)$ implies
the existence of $\sigma: s_i\mapsto t_i.$                                               

\medskip

Now let $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ and $\sigma^\mathrm{CM}$ be its restriction to  $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(\mathrm{CM}).$ By the claim there is $\rho^\mathrm{CM}\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}(\mathrm{CM})$ whose restriction to $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}(\mathrm{CM})$ is $\sigma^\mathrm{CM}.$ 

Since special points are Zariski dense in the components $\mathrm{S}^\mu_{K(N)},$ $\rho^\mathrm{CM}$ determines the unique bijective map  
$\mathrm{S}^\mu\to \mathrm{S}^{\rho^\mathrm{CM}(\mu)}$ on the set of components of $\mathrm{S}.$ More precisely, 
$$\rho^\mathrm{CM}(\mu)=\mu\cdot \lambda_{\rho}$$
where $\lambda_{\rho}=\det r_\tau(\rho^\mathrm{CM})\in \hat{{\mathbb Z}}^\times$ is obtained from the property (\ref{rsig}) of automorphisms acting on CM-points.

Consider an arbitrary $s\in \mathrm{S}_\approx.$ It follows from the definition of $\approx$ that for each component  $\mathrm{S}^\mu$ there is a unique 
$x\in \mathrm{S}^\mu$ such that $x_\approx=s.$ Call this element $x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu).$ 
By construction any element of $\mathrm{S}$ has the form $x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)$ for some
$s\in \mathrm{S}_\approx$ and a component $\mathrm{S}^\mu$ of $\mathrm{S}.$


Consider the element $\mathbf{t}\in \mathrm{GL}_2^+({\mathbb Q})$ and the set $\mathbf{t}^\Delta$  definable in $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ by definition. 
 Elements $\mathbf{t}^\mu$ of $\mathbf{t}^\Delta$ can be identified with curves $C^\mu_{\mathbf{t}/\approx}$ on $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}\times \tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ (see \ref{specpointsapprox}A(b)) and there is a one-to-one correspondence
between elements $\mathbf{t}^\mu$ of  $\mathbf{t}^\Delta$ and components $\mathrm{S}^\mu$ of $\mathrm{S}$   given by
$$C^\mu_{\mathbf{t}}=C_{\mathbf{t}}\cap (\mathrm{S}^\mu\times \mathrm{S}^\mu)$$
(see \ref{specpointsapprox}A).

Clearly, $$\rho^\mathrm{CM}: \mathbf{t}^\mu\mapsto \mathbf{t}^{ \rho^\mathrm{CM}(\mu)}=\sigma(\mathbf{t}^\mu)=\mathbf{t}^{ \sigma(\mu)},\ \ \mathbf{t}^{ \rho^\mathrm{CM}(\mu)}=\mathbf{t}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\rho}=\mathbf{t}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma}.$$
for $\sigma$ and $\rho^\mathrm{CM}$  as above. This gives us an extension of the action of $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ to components of $\mathrm{S},$ $$\sigma: \mathrm{S}^\mu \to \mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma}.$$ 


Define the map $$\rho: \mathrm{S}\to \mathrm{S}; \ \ x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)^\rho:= x(s^\sigma, \mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma}).$$
This is the lift of $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ to a transformation  $\rho$ of $\mathrm{S}$ and by definition the restriction of $\rho$ to the CM-substructure is $\rho^\mathrm{CM}$   above.

By construction $\rho$ respects the splitting of $\mathrm{S}$ into components. 

In order to prove that $\rho\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}$
it remains 
to prove that $\rho$ respects the action by elements of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f).$

Consider $h\in \Delta'({\mathbb Q}_+)\cdot \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f).$
By definition \ref{specpointsapprox}A(b)) via the action on $\mathrm{S}^\mu$  $h$ induces on $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}$ the transformation
$h^\mu.$ This means that
$$h\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)=x(h^\mu\cdot s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)$$
and thus
$$(h\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu))^\rho=x(h^\mu\cdot s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)^\rho=
x((h^{\mu}\cdot s)^\sigma, \mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma})=x(h^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma}\cdot s^\sigma, \mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma})=$$ $$=h\cdot x(s^\sigma, \mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma})=
h\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)^\rho$$
which proves that any such $h$ is invariant under $\rho.$


Next consider the action of an element $d$ of $\Delta(\mathbb{A}_f)$ on 
$x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu).$ Since any $a\in \mathbb{A}_f$ can be represented as $a=q\cdot \nu,$ for $q\in {\mathbb Q}_+$ and $\nu\in \hat{{\mathbb Z}}^\times,$
$d$ can be represented as 
$d=\mathbf{d}_q\cdot \mathbf{d}_\nu.$ Thus, the action by $d$ is invariant under $\rho$ if and only if the action by $\mathbf{d}_\nu$ is.                

We have by construction
$$\mathbf{d}_\nu\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu)=x(s,\mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot\nu})$$

Thus
$$(\mathbf{d}_\nu\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^\mu))^\rho= x(s,\mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot\nu}))^\rho=x(s^\sigma,\mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot\nu\cdot \lambda_\sigma})=\mathbf{d}_\nu\cdot x(s^\sigma,\mathrm{S}^{\mu\cdot \lambda_\sigma})=\mathbf{d}_\nu\cdot x(s,\mathrm{S}^{\mu})^\rho$$
which proves that the actions by $\mathbf{d}_\nu$ and by $d$ on $\mathrm{S}$ are invariant under $\rho.$

Since any element of $\mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$ can be represented in the form
$d\cdot h$ where $d\in \Delta(\mathbb{A}_f)$ and $h\in \mathrm{SL}_2(\mathbb{A}_f)$
we proved that $\rho$ satisfies (\ref{autg}) and thus $\rho\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}.$ $\rho$ is the lifting of $\sigma\in \mathrm{Aut}\, \tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$ to  $\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Pure}.$

This completes the proof of the theorem. $\Box$
head: manual
name: Claim

title: Definition
body_md:
$\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Full}$ is the expansion of $\tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Pure}$                                                                                
 defined over ${\mathbb Q},$ such that
  $$\mathrm{Aut}\, \tilde{\mathbb{H}}^\mathrm{Full}=\mathrm{Aut}\, \mathbf{S}^\mathrm{Full}.$$
head: manual

title: Proof
body_md:
See \ref{specpointsapprox}, A(b). 
\end{pkt}
